lines: You start a weekend business doing bike tune-ups at the farmers market. You charge 40 dollars, the parts cost 10, and the spot, tools and insurance cost 300 dollars a month. Your first month, 6 tune-ups, and you still lose money.
Revenue is price times the number sold. Fixed costs stay the same no matter how much you sell. Variable costs go up with every sale.
Profit is revenue minus all your costs. 25 tune-ups bring in 1,000 dollars. Take away 300 fixed and 250 for parts, and you keep 450 dollars.
Each tune-up leaves 40 minus 10, or 30 dollars. That's the contribution margin. It pays the fixed costs first, then becomes profit.
The break-even point is fixed costs divided by the contribution margin. 300 divided by 30 is 10 tune-ups a month. Number 11 is your first profit. If the answer has a decimal, round up.
Profit margin is profit divided by revenue. 450 out of 1,000 is 45 percent. And a higher price isn't always better: at 50 dollars, only 18 customers come, and profit drops to 420.
So: sort your costs, find what each sale adds, then divide and round up.
